references.text: Here we see the outcome of God's promise to spare the city if there were righteous people there. Although the cities were ultimately destroyed, Lot and his family were saved because of Abraham's intercession.

Moses intercedes for Israel after the golden calf incident, and God 'relents' from the disaster he had planned to bring. This is a strong parallel to Abraham's intercession for Sodom and God's willingness to spare the city on account of that prayer.

God asks Jeremiah to search through the streets of Jerusalem to find one person who does what is right and seeks truth, promising then to forgive the city—a direct parallel to God's promise to spare Sodom for the sake of the righteous.
God sought a man to stand in the gap for the land so that he would not destroy it, but found none. This connects to the theme of how the righteous influence God's judgment over a city.
The prophet Isaiah's call to repentance and God's willingness to forgive sinners recalls God's readiness to spare Sodom if there had been righteous people there.
James' letter on the power of a righteous person's prayer underscores the significance of Abraham's intercession for Sodom.
Peter's reference to Lot as a righteous man who was tormented by the immoral lifestyle of the lawless points back to God's assessment of Sodom and Gomorrah and his decision to spare the righteous.
Through the blessing of the righteous, a city is exalted—this principle lies at the heart of God's promise to spare all of Sodom for the sake of the righteous.
